name: TypeScript
title: TypeScript: JavaScript with types
intro: TypeScript is JavaScript with type annotations added. Microsoft released it in 2012, and it is now how most large web apps are written, from VS Code itself to the front ends of big sites. You say what kind of value each variable and parameter holds, and the TypeScript compiler, tsc, checks the whole program before it runs: a typo in a property name or a function called with the wrong thing is caught while you type, not by a user. Then tsc removes the types and writes plain JavaScript, so it runs anywhere JavaScript does. These lessons assume you know a little JavaScript (there is a course for that too) and use strict mode, which turns on all the checks. Every example passes the checker and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, install TypeScript with npm install -g typescript, save the example as hello.ts, and type tsc --strict hello.ts && node hello.js.

lessons.title: Types on values
lessons.summary: Annotations, inference, and what the checker catches.

sections.p: A type annotation goes after a name with a colon: let nuts: number = 7. The basic types are number, string and boolean, and arrays are written number[]. Once a variable has a type, giving it a value of another type is an error that tsc reports before the program runs. Here the commented line would be refused with Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

You rarely need to write every type. When a variable starts with a value, TypeScript infers its type from that value, so let count = 3 is a number without saying so. Hover over a name in an editor like VS Code to see what was inferred. const goes one step further: const day = "sat" has the type "sat", the one exact string, because it can never change.

TypeScript's types exist only for the checker. tsc strips them out and the JavaScript that runs has none, so typeof at run time still answers with JavaScript's own small set of names. This also means a type can't check data that arrives while the program runs, such as JSON from a server; the lesson on unions shows how to check such data yourself.

practice.why: total is inferred as a number, so += adds. There are three items.

practice.q: What does tsc do with  let nuts: number = "lots";  ?
practice.why: The checker compares the value's type with the annotation before anything runs.

practice.q: What is the type of day after  const day = "sat";  ?
practice.why: A const can never change, so TypeScript gives it the exact literal type. With let it would widen to string.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Typed parameters, return types, optional and default parameters.

sections.p: Parameters always need types, because TypeScript can't guess what callers will pass. The return type goes after the brackets; it can usually be inferred, but writing it documents the function and catches a wrong return. A ? makes a parameter optional, and a default value does the same while giving it a value.

A function's type is written like an arrow: (n: number) => number is a function that takes a number and returns one. Passing a function with the wrong shape is an error. In arrow functions passed straight to something like map, TypeScript already knows the parameter type, so you can leave it off.

practice.why: The default is used when the second argument is left out. greeting's type, string, is inferred from the default.

practice.q: In  label(tree: string, count?: number) , what is count's type inside the function?
practice.why: An optional parameter may be missing, so TypeScript makes you handle undefined before treating it as a number.

lessons.title: Object types
lessons.summary: type and interface, optional and readonly properties, structural typing.

sections.p: An object's type lists its properties and their types. You can name one with type or with interface; for plain object shapes they work almost the same. ? marks a property that may be missing and readonly one that can't be changed after the object is made. Misspelling a property, or leaving out a required one, is an error.

TypeScript compares types by their shape: any object with the right properties fits, whatever it was called or wherever it came from. This is called structural typing, and it matches how JavaScript code already passes plain objects around.

practice.why: The acorn has no grams, so ?? gives 1 in its place: 3 + 1.

practice.q: Why can nest, which has a tree property too, be passed where a Point is expected?
options: It has x and y numbers, and that is all Point asks for
It can't; that line is an error
practice.answer: It has x and y numbers, and that is all Point asks for
practice.why: Structural typing checks that the needed properties are there. Only an object literal written straight into the call gets an extra check for unknown properties.

lessons.title: Unions and narrowing
lessons.summary: A | B, literal types, narrowing with typeof and tags, never.

sections.p: A union type, written string | number, means the value is one of those types. Before you can use something only one of them has, you must check which it is. TypeScript follows your if and typeof checks and narrows the type inside each branch.
sections.out:
text of length 5
number doubled is 42

sections.p: Unions of string literals, like "spring" | "autumn", list every allowed value. Give each kind of object a kind property with its own literal, and a switch on kind narrows to the right shape. Assigning the leftover value to never in the default branch makes the checker tell you if a new kind is added and not handled.

Data parsed at run time, such as JSON, has no checked type. Give it the type unknown, which allows nothing until you check it, and narrow it step by step. A function whose return type is v is Nut is a type guard: when it returns true, TypeScript treats the value as a Nut from then on.

practice.why: Array.isArray narrows v to string[] in the if branch, so the list of two gives 2 * 10.

options: Values whose type must be checked before use
practice.answer: Values whose type must be checked before use
practice.why: unknown accepts any value but lets you do nothing with it until you narrow it. any skips the checks entirely.

lessons.title: Generics
lessons.summary: Type parameters, Array<T>, Record and the utility types.

sections.p: A generic function has a type parameter in angle brackets, <T>, standing for whatever type the caller uses. The return type can then depend on it: first of a string[] is a string, and of a number[] a number. TypeScript usually infers T from the arguments.

Many built-in types are generic. Array<T> is another way to write T[], Map<K, V> maps keys to values, and Record<K, V> is an object with keys of type K. The utility types build new types from old ones: Partial<T> makes every property optional and Pick<T, K> keeps only some.

practice.why: T is number for the first call and string for the second, so * and repeat both type-check.

options: An object with any of Squirrel's properties, all optional
A Squirrel that can't be changed
practice.answer: An object with any of Squirrel's properties, all optional
practice.why: Partial adds ? to every property, which suits a list of changes.

lessons.title: Classes and async code
lessons.summary: Access modifiers, implements, and typed promises.

sections.p: Classes work as in JavaScript, with types added. private fields can be used only inside the class, and the checker enforces it. Writing private or readonly before a constructor parameter declares the field and fills it in one step. implements checks that a class has everything an interface asks for.

An async function returns a Promise, and its type says what the promise will hold: Promise<number>. await waits for it and gives you the number. Promise.all waits for several at once and keeps their types in order.

practice.why: Each object has its own private count. a has ticked twice and b once.
main runs up to the await and then lets the rest of the script go on, so "first" prints before the awaited result.

lessons.title: Errors and unknown
lessons.summary: try and catch with unknown, error classes, and results as values.

sections.p: In strict mode the variable in catch (err) has the type unknown, because anything can be thrown, not just Error objects. You can't use an unknown value until you narrow it, usually with instanceof Error. That forces you to handle the odd case where someone threw a string.
sections.out:
count 12
error: not a count: "twelve"
error: not a count: "-3"

sections.p: A class that extends Error carries extra fields, and instanceof tells your errors apart from everyone else's. Set name so the error prints with a useful label.
sections.out:
StashFullError 2 the stash holds at most 2 nuts
acorn, walnut

sections.p: A union type can say "this worked, here's the value" or "this failed, here's why". The caller has to look at ok before it can reach value, so a failure can't be forgotten the way an uncaught exception can.

practice.q: What type does err have in catch (err) under strict mode?
practice.why: Anything can be thrown, so TypeScript makes you narrow it before use.
An Oops is also an Error, because Oops extends Error.
Only the two ok results have n, and checking r.ok narrows the type so r.n is allowed.

lessons.title: keyof, typeof and as const
lessons.summary: Types taken from values, so the two never drift apart.

sections.p: typeof in a type position gives the type of a value, and keyof gives the union of an object type's keys. Together they let a function accept only the keys an object really has: a typo is caught by the checker.

as const freezes a value's type to exactly what is written: an array of strings becomes a readonly tuple of those literal strings. Indexing it with number then gives a union of the entries, a neat way to keep a list and its type in one place.
satisfies checks a value against a type without widening it. Below, every entry must be a number, and a misspelt key would be refused, but stock.acorn keeps its own precise type.

practice.q: With const p = { a: 1, b: 2 }, what is keyof typeof p?
practice.why: typeof p is the object's type, and keyof takes the union of its keys.
"M" is at index 1, so 1 + 1 is 2, and the tuple has three entries.

practice.q: What does as const do to ["x", "y"]?
options: Makes it a readonly tuple of the literal types "x" and "y"
Nothing at run time or in types
practice.answer: Makes it a readonly tuple of the literal types "x" and "y"
practice.why: It changes only the type; the JavaScript value is the same array.

lessons.title: Mapped and conditional types
lessons.summary: Types built from other types: how Partial and friends work.

sections.p: A mapped type walks over the keys of another type and builds a new property for each: { [K in keyof T]: ... }. The built-in Partial, Readonly and Record are written this way. Here is a type that turns every property into a function that returns it.
A extends B ? X : Y picks a type by testing another. With infer it can pull a piece out: below, ElementOf gives the element type of an array type, and never for anything else.
Types can be built from strings, too. `on${Capitalize}` turns each event name into a handler name, and a mapped type with as renames the keys.

practice.q: Which built-in type is { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }?
practice.why: The ? after the key makes every property optional.

practice.q: What is ElementOf<boolean[]> with type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never?
practice.why: boolean[] matches (infer E)[], so E is boolean.
Only a is true; filter(Boolean) keeps the true values.

lessons.title: Project: a typed nut inventory
lessons.summary: Tagged unions, a reducer, Result values and a report together.

sections.p: An inventory is built by replaying a list of events. Each event is one case of a tagged union, so the switch must handle every kind; the never check at the end makes tsc complain if a new kind is added and forgotten. Taking more nuts than you have is a failure returned as a value, not thrown.
sections.out:
skipped: cannot gift 5 walnut: only 3
acorn      5
hazelnut   4
walnut     3
gifts to: Pip

sections.p: Add a "traded" event that swaps one nut for another and see tsc point at the unhandled case, read the events from a JSON file with node:fs, or keep a history of every stock along the way.

practice.q: Why does the default branch assign e to a variable of type never?
options: So tsc reports an error if a new event kind isn't handled
To throw an error at run time
To convert e to a string
practice.answer: So tsc reports an error if a new event kind isn't handled
practice.why: After every case is handled, e has type never; a new kind would not be assignable to never.

options: Only the gift case of the union
practice.answer: Only the gift case of the union
practice.why: Extract keeps the members of a union that are assignable to the second type.
The spread makes a new object, so changing next leaves stock alone.
